claim: The study was conducted in six villages in Maprik district, East Sepik Province, PNG between August 2009 and May 2010.
source: This study was conducted in six villages in Maprik district, East Sepik Province, PNG between August 2009 and May 2010 (Robinson et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the location and time period of the study with a citation to Robinson et al., 2015.

claim: 524 children aged 5–10 years were enrolled in the study.
source: 524 children aged 5–10 years were enrolled and randomized to receive either chloroquine (CQ), artemeter-lumefantrine (AL) and primaquine (PQ); or CQ, AL and placebo.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number and age range of enrolled children.

claim: 466 children completed the full course of randomized treatment and were followed for 8 months.
source: Demographic parameters of the 466 children that completed the full course of randomized treatment with PQ/CQ/AL (n = 233) or placebo/CQ/AL (n = 233), and were thereafter closely followed for 8 months, were comparable between the six villages (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of children who completed treatment and follow-up duration.

claim: P. vivax was the most common infection at enrolment with 48% of children positive by qPCR.
source: P. vivax was the most common infection at enrolment with 48% of children positive by quantitative PCR (qPCR), followed by P. falciparum (24%), P. malariae (15%) and P. ovale (3%; Table 2).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific prevalence data from qPCR testing at enrolment, with reference to Table 2.

claim: P. falciparum prevalence at enrolment was 24%.
source: P. vivax was the most common infection at enrolment with 48% of children positive by quantitative PCR (qPCR), followed by P. falciparum (24%), P. malariae (15%) and P. ovale (3%; Table 2).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific prevalence data from qPCR testing at enrolment.

claim: 39% of children were not infected with any Plasmodium species at enrolment.
source: 39% of children were not infected with any Plasmodium species at enrolment.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the proportion of uninfected children at baseline.

claim: Children who received PQ experienced similar numbers of new blood-stage infections with P. falciparum and P. vivax during follow-up.
source: Children who had received PQ for clearance of P. vivax hypnozoites experienced similar numbers of new blood-stage infections with P. falciparum and P. vivax during follow-up (mean Pf-molFOB = 1.5 CI95 [1.3–1.7] new blood-stage clones/year, Pv-molFOB = 1.6 [1.4–1.9] new blood-stage clones/year, Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific molFOB values for both species in the PQ arm with confidence intervals and references to figures.

claim: Pv-molFOB in the placebo arm showed a pronounced peak at months 2–3 of follow-up.
source: Pv-molFOB in the placebo arm showed a pronounced peak at months 2–3 of follow-up, which likely represents a wave of fast-relapsing hypnozoites in children who did not receive PQ (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes temporal patterns in Pv-molFOB with reference to Figure 1A and provides an interpretation.

claim: The peak in Pv-molFOB at months 2-3 in the placebo arm likely represents a wave of fast-relapsing hypnozoites.
source: Pv-molFOB in the placebo arm showed a pronounced peak at months 2–3 of follow-up, which likely represents a wave of fast-relapsing hypnozoites in children who did not receive PQ (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the observed peak based on the study design.

claim: P. vivax prevalence in the PQ arm was comparable to P. falciparum prevalence throughout the study.
source: P. vivax prevalence in the PQ arm was comparable to P. falciparum prevalence throughout the study and increased steadily, irrespective of the diagnostic method used (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: The manuscript describes prevalence patterns with reference to figures showing temporal trends.

claim: At the end of follow-up, P. vivax prevalence by qPCR in the placebo arm was 25% [19–31%].
source: At the end of follow-up, P. vivax prevalence by qPCR in the placebo arm was 25% [19–31%], and therefore more than two-fold higher than in the PQ arm (9% [6–14%]; Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific prevalence values with confidence intervals at the end of follow-up.

claim: At the end of follow-up, P. vivax prevalence by qPCR in the PQ arm was 9% [6–14%].
source: At the end of follow-up, P. vivax prevalence by qPCR in the placebo arm was 25% [19–31%], and therefore more than two-fold higher than in the PQ arm (9% [6–14%]; Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific prevalence values with confidence intervals at the end of follow-up.

claim: At least 50% of the overall P. vivax prevalence in this cohort can be attributed to the contribution of relapses.
source: Also, throughout follow-up, P. vivax prevalence in the placebo arm was 2–3 fold higher compared to the PQ arm, suggesting that at least 50% of the overall P. vivax prevalence in this cohort can be attributed to the contribution of relapses.
evidence: The manuscript provides an inference based on the comparison of prevalence between treatment arms.

claim: Village of residence was a main predictor for the risk of recurrent Plasmodium spp. during follow-up.
source: After adjusting for the effect of PQ treatment (Robinson et al., 2015), village of residence and infection status by qPCR at enrolment were the main predictors for the risk of recurrent Plasmodium spp. during follow-up (Table 3).
evidence: The manuscript states the results of multivariable analysis with reference to Table 3.

claim: Infection status by qPCR at enrolment was a main predictor for the risk of recurrent Plasmodium spp. during follow-up.
source: After adjusting for the effect of PQ treatment (Robinson et al., 2015), village of residence and infection status by qPCR at enrolment were the main predictors for the risk of recurrent Plasmodium spp. during follow-up (Table 3).
evidence: The manuscript states the results of multivariable analysis with reference to Table 3.

claim: The risk of recurrent P. falciparum was reduced by 27% [0–48%] after PQ treatment (p=0.064).
source: Interestingly, in addition to a protective effect against recurrent P. vivax and P. ovale, the risk of recurrent P. falciparum was also reduced by 27% [0–48%] after PQ treatment (p=0.064).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific risk reduction values with confidence intervals and p-value.

claim: Malaria transmission showed high micro-spatial heterogeneity with more than 10-fold differences in Pf- and Pv-molFOB between villages.
source: Malaria transmission showed high micro-spatial heterogeneity with more than 10-fold differences in Pf- and Pv-molFOB (in the PQ arm) between villages despite an overall high LLIN use by the study participants (during follow-up; village average use,>90%; individual use,>50%).
evidence: The manuscript describes the magnitude of heterogeneity observed in molFOB between villages.

claim: Overall LLIN use during follow-up was high with village average use >90% and individual use >50%.
source: Malaria transmission showed high micro-spatial heterogeneity with more than 10-fold differences in Pf- and Pv-molFOB (in the PQ arm) between villages despite an overall high LLIN use by the study participants (during follow-up; village average use,>90%; individual use,>50%).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific data on LLIN use during the study.

claim: A total of 98 clinical malaria episodes were observed during the study period.
source: A total of 98 clinical malaria episodes, here defined as fever plus presence of LM-detectable parasites, were observed during the study period.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the total number of clinical episodes observed.

claim: 64 (65%) of the 98 clinical episodes exceeded the previously established pyrogenic thresholds.
source: Of these, 64 (65%) exceeded the previously established pyrogenic thresholds of 2500 and 500 parasites/µl per LM for P. falciparum and P. vivax, respectively (Mueller et al., 2009b).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts and percentages with citation to established thresholds.

claim: P. falciparum was the most common cause of clinical malaria episodes with 64 clinical episodes.
source: P. falciparum was the most common cause of clinical malaria episodes (P. falciparum, 64 clinical episodes; P. vivax, 31 clinical episodes; mixed P. falciparum/P. vivax by LM, 3 clinical episodes), despite lower incidence of new P. falciparum blood-stage clones compared with P. vivax (P. falciparum, 342 new P. falciparum blood-stage clones; P. vivax, 849 new blood-stage clones).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts of clinical episodes by species.

claim: 31 P. vivax clinical episodes were observed during the study.
source: P. falciparum was the most common cause of clinical malaria episodes (P. falciparum, 64 clinical episodes; P. vivax, 31 clinical episodes; mixed P. falciparum/P. vivax by LM, 3 clinical episodes), despite lower incidence of new P. falciparum blood-stage clones compared with P. vivax (P. falciparum, 342 new P. falciparum blood-stage clones; P. vivax, 849 new blood-stage clones).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts of clinical episodes by species.

claim: 342 new P. falciparum blood-stage clones were detected during the study.
source: P. falciparum was the most common cause of clinical malaria episodes (P. falciparum, 64 clinical episodes; P. vivax, 31 clinical episodes; mixed P. falciparum/P. vivax by LM, 3 clinical episodes), despite lower incidence of new P. falciparum blood-stage clones compared with P. vivax (P. falciparum, 342 new P. falciparum blood-stage clones; P. vivax, 849 new blood-stage clones).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts of new blood-stage clones detected.

claim: 849 new P. vivax blood-stage clones were detected during the study.
source: P. falciparum was the most common cause of clinical malaria episodes (P. falciparum, 64 clinical episodes; P. vivax, 31 clinical episodes; mixed P. falciparum/P. vivax by LM, 3 clinical episodes), despite lower incidence of new P. falciparum blood-stage clones compared with P. vivax (P. falciparum, 342 new P. falciparum blood-stage clones; P. vivax, 849 new blood-stage clones).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts of new blood-stage clones detected.

claim: Clinical incidence rate was 0.28 [0.21–0.35] P. falciparum episodes/year.
source: Including clinical episodes with mixed infection as determined by LM in the estimates for both species, clinical incidence rate (IR) was 0.28 [0.21–0.35] P. falciparum episodes/year and 0.12 [0.08–0.17] P. vivax episodes/year.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific incidence rates with confidence intervals.

claim: Clinical incidence rate was 0.12 [0.08–0.17] P. vivax episodes/year.
source: Including clinical episodes with mixed infection as determined by LM in the estimates for both species, clinical incidence rate (IR) was 0.28 [0.21–0.35] P. falciparum episodes/year and 0.12 [0.08–0.17] P. vivax episodes/year.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific incidence rates with confidence intervals.

claim: At least one new blood-stage clone was detected in 70% (47/67) of samples from P. falciparum clinical episodes.
source: At least one new blood-stage clone was detected in 70% (47/67) of samples from P. falciparum and 71% (24/34) of samples from P. vivax clinical episodes.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific proportions of clinical episodes with new clones.

claim: At least one new blood-stage clone was detected in 71% (24/34) of samples from P. vivax clinical episodes.
source: At least one new blood-stage clone was detected in 70% (47/67) of samples from P. falciparum and 71% (24/34) of samples from P. vivax clinical episodes.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific proportions of clinical episodes with new clones.

claim: Pv-molFOB was positively associated with the risk of clinical episodes with each additional blood-stage P. vivax clone increasing the risk (AHR = 1.07 [1.04–1.09], p<0.001).
source: On an individual level, Pv-molFOB was positively associated with the risk of clinical episodes and each additional blood-stage P. vivax clone increased the risk of experiencing a P. vivax clinical episode slightly (AHR = 1.07 [1.04–1.09], p<0.001; Table 5).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific hazard ratios with confidence intervals and p-values from statistical analysis.

claim: The risk for a P. vivax clinical episode decreased significantly with age (AHR = 0.62 [0.46–0.84], p=0.002).
source: The risk for a P. vivax clinical episode decreased significantly with age (AHR = 0.62 [0.46–0.84], p=0.002; Table 5).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific hazard ratios with confidence intervals and p-values from statistical analysis.

claim: P. vivax densities decreased with age (by qPCR, exp(β)=0.90 [0.83–0.98], p=0.016).
source: This was paralleled by a decrease in P. vivax densities with age (by qPCR, exp(β)=0.90 [0.83–0.98], p=0.016; Supplementary file 3) indicative of more advanced immunity against P. vivax and thus better control of P. vivax densities in older children.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific statistical results with confidence intervals and p-values.

claim: The decrease in P. vivax densities with age is indicative of more advanced immunity against P. vivax in older children.
source: This was paralleled by a decrease in P. vivax densities with age (by qPCR, exp(β)=0.90 [0.83–0.98], p=0.016; Supplementary file 3) indicative of more advanced immunity against P. vivax and thus better control of P. vivax densities in older children.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the observed age-related decrease in parasite density.

claim: No age-dependent decrease in the incidence of clinical episodes was observed for P. falciparum.
source: In sharp contrast to the age-dependent decline of P. vivax clinical episode incidence, no age-dependent decrease in the incidence of clinical episodes was observed for P. falciparum.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the absence of an age effect for P. falciparum clinical episodes.

claim: Pf-molFOB was positively associated with the risk of clinical episodes with each additional P. falciparum blood-stage clone increasing the risk (AHR = 1.15 [1.11–1.21], p<0.001).
source: Overall, Pv-molFOB was positively associated with the risk of clinical episodes and each additional P. falciparum blood-stage clone slightly increased the risk for P. falciparum clinical episodes (AHR = 1.15 [1.11–1.21], p<0.001; Table 5)
evidence: The manuscript provides specific hazard ratios with confidence intervals and p-values from statistical analysis.

claim: The proportion of P. falciparum clinical episodes relative to new infections decreased with increasing exposure.
source: Although no age trends were observed for P. falciparum in this cohort, when children were stratified into groups ranging from low to high exposure we found that the proportion of P. falciparum clinical episodes relative to new infections decreased with increasing exposure.
evidence: The manuscript describes patterns observed when stratifying by exposure level.

claim: One clinical episode per three new blood-stage clones was detected in the least exposed children (Pf-molFOB <4 new blood-stage clones/year).
source: One clinical episode per three new blood-stage clones was detected in the least exposed children (Pf-molFOB <4 new blood-stage clones/year), but only one clinical episode per 15 blood-stage clones in the highest exposed children (Pf-molFOB >9 new blood-stage clones/year, Fisher's exact test p<0.001).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific ratios of clinical episodes to new infections by exposure category with statistical test results.

claim: Only one clinical episode per 15 blood-stage clones was detected in the highest exposed children (Pf-molFOB >9 new blood-stage clones/year).
source: One clinical episode per three new blood-stage clones was detected in the least exposed children (Pf-molFOB <4 new blood-stage clones/year), but only one clinical episode per 15 blood-stage clones in the highest exposed children (Pf-molFOB >9 new blood-stage clones/year, Fisher's exact test p<0.001).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific ratios of clinical episodes to new infections by exposure category with statistical test results.

claim: LLIN use at enrolment was associated with a 56% [13–78%] reduced risk of P. falciparum clinical episodes (p=0.018).
source: LLIN use at enrolment was associated with a 56% [13–78%] reduced risk of P. falciparum clinical episodes (p=0.018; Table 5).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific risk reduction values with confidence intervals and p-values.

claim: A higher risk for P. falciparum clinical episodes was observed in children that had received PQ treatment (AHR = 1.79 [1.05–3.03], p=0.031).
source: A higher risk for P. falciparum clinical episodes in children that had received PQ treatment for clearance of P. vivax liver stages was observed (AHR = 1.79 [1.05–3.03], p=0.031; Table 5), suggesting a potential protective effect of P. vivax infections against P. falciparum clinical episodes.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific hazard ratios with confidence intervals and p-values from statistical analysis.

claim: A concurrent or recent infection with P. vivax reduced the odds of a P. falciparum clinical episode by 65% [22-85%] (p=0.011).
source: Analysis to further explore this revealed that a concurrent or recent infection (i.e., at the same or preceding follow-up visit) with P. vivax reduced the odds of a P. falciparum clinical episode by 65% [22-85%] (p=0.011; Table 6).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific odds reduction values with confidence intervals and p-values from statistical analysis.

claim: P. falciparum parasite densities were reduced by 55% [19–75%] (p=0.008) in mixed P. falciparum/P. vivax infections compared to P. falciparum single infections.
source: Further indications for a potential interaction between the two species was also observed when analyzing P. falciparum parasite densities, which were reduced by 55% [19–75%] (p=0.008; Supplementary file 3) in mixed P. falciparum/P. vivax infections compared to P. falciparum single infections, indicative of suppression of one of the species in mixed infections.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific density reduction values with confidence intervals and p-values from statistical analysis.

claim: The reduction in P. falciparum densities in mixed infections is indicative of suppression of one of the species in mixed infections.
source: Further indications for a potential interaction between the two species was also observed when analyzing P. falciparum parasite densities, which were reduced by 55% [19–75%] (p=0.008; Supplementary file 3) in mixed P. falciparum/P. vivax infections compared to P. falciparum single infections, indicative of suppression of one of the species in mixed infections.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the observed density reduction in mixed infections.

claim: P. vivax and P. falciparum PCR-prevalence in the general population was reduced from 32% and 39% in 2006 to 13% and 18% in 2010.
source: P. vivax and P. falciparum PCR-prevalence in the general population was reduced from 32% and 39% in 2006 to 13% and 18% in 2010 (Koepfli et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites specific prevalence data from a previous study by Koepfli et al., 2015.

claim: Malaria prevalence has sharply declined in PNG in the last decade, largely as a result of two nationwide distributions of long-lasting insecticide treated bednets (LLIN).
source: In Papua New Guinea (PNG), malaria prevalence has sharply declined in the last decade, largely as a result of two nationwide distributions of long-lasting insecticide treated bednets (LLIN) (Hetzel et al., 2015; Hetzel et al., 2014; Hetzel et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies attributing the decline in malaria prevalence to LLIN distributions.

claim: Prior to the up-scaling of malaria control, P. vivax endemicity in PNG was among the highest worldwide.
source: Prior to the up-scaling of malaria control, P. vivax endemicity in PNG was among the highest worldwide (Hetzel et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study describing historical P. vivax endemicity levels in PNG.

claim: Clinical immunity to P. vivax was acquired very rapidly in PNG children.
source: Clinical immunity to P. vivax was acquired very rapidly in PNG children, and the incidence of P. vivax clinical episodes peaked in children younger than two years with only very few P. vivax clinical episodes reported in children older than 5 years or adults (Genton et al., 2008; Michon et al., 2007; Lin et al., 2010; Betuela et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies describing the rapid acquisition of P. vivax immunity in PNG children.

claim: The incidence of P. vivax clinical episodes peaked in children younger than two years.
source: Clinical immunity to P. vivax was acquired very rapidly in PNG children, and the incidence of P. vivax clinical episodes peaked in children younger than two years with only very few P. vivax clinical episodes reported in children older than 5 years or adults (Genton et al., 2008; Michon et al., 2007; Lin et al., 2010; Betuela et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies describing age patterns in P. vivax clinical episodes.

claim: The risk for uncomplicated P. falciparum clinical episodes increased during early childhood.
source: In contrast, the risk for uncomplicated P. falciparum clinical episodes increased during early childhood (Lin et al., 2010) and significant reductions in incidence of clinical episodes or high-density infections were only observed in children aged 5 years and older (Michon et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies describing age patterns in P. falciparum clinical episodes.

claim: The molecular force of blood-stage infection (molFOB) describes the number of new genotypes observed in consecutive blood samples from cohort participants over time.
source: The molecular force of blood-stage infection (molFOB) describes the number of new genotypes observed in consecutive blood samples from cohort participants over time (Mueller et al., 2012; Koepfli et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript defines molFOB with citations to previous studies.

claim: For P. falciparum, molFOB is closely linked to the number of infective mosquito bites and therefore is a direct proxy for the actual force of infection (FOI).
source: For P. falciparum, molFOB is closely linked to the number of infective mosquito bites and therefore is a direct proxy for the actual force of infection (FOI) and thus for transmission in endemic settings (Smith et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study establishing the relationship between Pf-molFOB and force of infection.

claim: For P. vivax, molFOB is a compound measure of exposure to newly acquired infections from mosquito bites and relapsing blood-stage infections.
source: For P. vivax, clones appearing in the blood-stream can either originate directly from an infective mosquito bite or from a relapsing liver hypnozoite (Koepfli et al., 2013). For P. vivax, molFOB is thus a compound measure of exposure to newly acquired infections from mosquito bites and relapsing blood-stage infections.
evidence: The manuscript explains the composite nature of Pv-molFOB with citation.

claim: The usefulness of molFOB as a surrogate marker of individual exposure was validated originally in a cohort of young PNG children 1–4 years of age.
source: The usefulness of molFOB as a surrogate marker of individual exposure was validated originally in a cohort of young PNG children 1–4 years of age, in which species-specific molFOB was the most important predictor of clinical incidence for both species (Mueller et al., 2012; Koepfli et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous validation studies of molFOB.

claim: Species-specific molFOB was the most important predictor of clinical incidence for both species in a cohort of young PNG children 1–4 years of age.
source: The usefulness of molFOB as a surrogate marker of individual exposure was validated originally in a cohort of young PNG children 1–4 years of age, in which species-specific molFOB was the most important predictor of clinical incidence for both species (Mueller et al., 2012; Koepfli et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies showing molFOB as a predictor of clinical incidence.

claim: The study received ethical clearance from the PNG IMR Institutional Review Board (0908), the PNG Medical Advisory Committee (09.11), and the Ethics Committee of Basel 237/11.
source: The study received ethical clearance from the PNG IMR Institutional Review Board (0908), the PNG Medical Advisory Committee (09.11), the Ethics Committee of Basel 237/11 and was conducted in full concordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the ethical approvals obtained.

claim: The study was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT02143934).
source: The study was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT02143934).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the trial registration number.

claim: All blood samples were examined by LM and qPCR for detection and speciation of Plasmodium infections.
source: All blood samples were examined by LM and qPCR for detection and speciation of Plasmodium infections as described earlier (Robinson et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript describes the diagnostic methods used with citation.

claim: The qPCR limit of detection (LOD) was 2 target copies/µl DNA, equaling 4 target copies/reaction, for all qPCRs.
source: The qPCR limit of detection (LOD) was determined using a standard plasmid dilution row and defined as the last point with more than 50% of replicates positive. The LOD was 2 target copies/µl DNA, equaling 4 target copies/reaction, for all qPCRs.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific technical details about the qPCR assay performance.

claim: Individual parasite clones were distinguished by genotyping the length-polymorphic Pf-msp2 or Pv-msp1F3 marker genes using capillary electrophoresis.
source: In all samples positive in P. falciparum and/or P. vivax qPCRs, individual parasite clones were distinguished by genotyping the length-polymorphic Pf-msp2 or Pv-msp1F3 marker genes using capillary electrophoresis for highly precise fragment sizing (Koepfli et al., 2013; Koepfli et al., 2011; Falk et al., 2006; Schoepflin et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript describes the genotyping methods used with citations.

claim: A new infection was defined as a Pf-msp2 or Pv-msp1F3 allele not present in the two preceding genotyping-positive samples.
source: A new infection was defined as a Pf-msp2 or Pv-msp1F3 allele not present in the two preceding genotyping-positive samples collected during active or passive surveillance (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly defines the criteria for identifying new infections.

claim: 430 (92.3%) of the 466 analyzed children completed the whole follow-up period.
source: This resulted in an analyzed population of 466 children (characterized in Table 1) of which 430 (92.3%) completed the whole follow-up period, with a median of 15 (IQR: 13–17) study contacts and mean TAR of 186 days (IQR 168–223 days).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific data on study completion rates.

claim: The median number of study contacts was 15 (IQR: 13–17).
source: This resulted in an analyzed population of 466 children (characterized in Table 1) of which 430 (92.3%) completed the whole follow-up period, with a median of 15 (IQR: 13–17) study contacts and mean TAR of 186 days (IQR 168–223 days).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific data on study contacts.

claim: Mean time at risk (TAR) was 186 days (IQR 168–223 days).
source: This resulted in an analyzed population of 466 children (characterized in Table 1) of which 430 (92.3%) completed the whole follow-up period, with a median of 15 (IQR: 13–17) study contacts and mean TAR of 186 days (IQR 168–223 days).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific data on time at risk.

claim: A malaria clinical episode was defined as fever (>37.5°C axillary) plus the presence of LM-detectable parasites.
source: For statistical analysis, a malaria clinical episode was defined as fever (>37.5°C axillary) plus the presence of LM-detectable parasites, irrespective of RDT result or antimalarial treatment during the field visit.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly defines the criteria for clinical episodes used in analysis.

claim: Assuming equal transmission from mosquitoes for both species, P. vivax relapses have contributed to a P. vivax prevalence twice as high as that of P. falciparum.
source: Assuming equal transmission from mosquitoes for both species, which was corroborated by a comparable Pf-molFOB and Pv-molFOB in the PQ arm, P. vivax relapses have contributed to a P. vivax prevalence twice as high as that of P. falciparum.
evidence: The manuscript provides an inference based on the comparison of molFOB and prevalence between species.

claim: Recent entomological data from Dreikikir district found similar sporozoite rates for P. falciparum and P. vivax.
source: Our molecular results thus support recent entomological data from Dreikikir district, 50 km from Maprik in East Sepik Province (Reimer et al., 2016) as well as earlier studies in East Sepik (Hii et al., 2001) that found similar sporozoite rates for P. falciparum and P. vivax.
evidence: The manuscript cites entomological studies supporting the molecular findings.

claim: P. vivax relapses accounted for more than half of the observed P. vivax prevalence in this cohort.
source: P. vivax relapses accounted for more than half of the observed P. vivax prevalence in this cohort, which is lower than what was previously estimated as the contribution of relapses towards Pv-molFOB by comparison of treatment arms (77%, Robinson et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript provides an estimate of the contribution of relapses to prevalence with comparison to a previous estimate.

claim: The contribution of relapses to P. vivax prevalence (more than half) is lower than the previously estimated contribution of relapses towards Pv-molFOB (77%).
source: P. vivax relapses accounted for more than half of the observed P. vivax prevalence in this cohort, which is lower than what was previously estimated as the contribution of relapses towards Pv-molFOB by comparison of treatment arms (77%, Robinson et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript compares two different estimates of relapse contribution with citation.

claim: The blood-stage antimalarial at baseline may have either triggered P. vivax relapses directly, or indirectly by allowing more hypnozoites to establish blood-stage infections in parasite-free hosts.
source: It is thus conceivable that the blood-stage antimalarial at baseline either triggered P. vivax relapses directly, or indirectly by allowing more hypnozoites to establish blood-stage infections in parasite-free hosts.
evidence: The manuscript proposes potential mechanisms for the observed relapse patterns.

claim: Blood-stage P. vivax infections from hypnozoites relapsing shortly after baseline treatment may be suppressed to sub-detectable densities until complete waning of drug levels.
source: Alternatively, blood-stage P. vivax infections from hypnozoites relapsing shortly after baseline treatment (during a period when antimalarial drugs were present at sub-curative levels) may be suppressed to sub-detectable densities until complete waning of drug levels, resulting in simultaneous proliferation and detection of many new blood-stage clones within the first weeks after treatment (Douglas et al., 2011; Tarning et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript proposes an alternative mechanism with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Children living in Bolumita had a modestly lower LLIN use compared to children from other villages.
source: Children living in Bolumita, where both P. falciparum and P. vivax molFOB and prevalence were highest, had a modestly lower LLIN use (mean during follow-up, 92%; at enrolment, 77%) compared to children from other villages (mean during follow-up, 97–100%; at enrolment, 91–100%).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific LLIN use data by village.

claim: LLIN use in the Bolumita community may be less effective in reducing malaria transmission.
source: It is conceivable that LLIN use in the Bolumita community may be less effective in reducing malaria transmission (Killeen et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript proposes a potential explanation with citations to relevant literature.

claim: Small-scale variations in vector species and distribution between and within villages in PNG have been described previously.
source: Small-scale variations in vector species and distribution between and within villages in PNG have been described previously (Cattani et al., 1986; Reimer et al., 2016; Charlwood et al., 1986; Hii et al., 1997; Burkot et al., 1988) and likely account in a large part for the micro-geographic heterogeneity in malariological parameters observed in this and other studies.
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies describing vector heterogeneity in PNG.

claim: Small-scale variations in vector species and distribution likely account in large part for the micro-geographic heterogeneity in malariological parameters observed in this study.
source: Small-scale variations in vector species and distribution between and within villages in PNG have been described previously (Cattani et al., 1986; Reimer et al., 2016; Charlwood et al., 1986; Hii et al., 1997; Burkot et al., 1988) and likely account in a large part for the micro-geographic heterogeneity in malariological parameters observed in this and other studies.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation linking vector heterogeneity to observed patterns.

claim: The overall estimates of molFOB may be biased due to imperfect detectability of clones.
source: The overall estimates of molFOB presented here may thus be biased.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges a potential limitation in molFOB estimation.

claim: Clonal detectability has been shown to decrease with age and MOI.
source: However, although clonal detectability has been shown to decrease with age (Felger et al., 2012; Sama et al., 2006) and MOI (Koepfli et al., 2011), it is unlikely to vary substantially within our cohort's age range and transmission setting.
evidence: The manuscript cites studies showing factors affecting clonal detectability.

claim: The observed differences in molFOB are likely to accurately reflect the relative differences in individual exposure as well as in population transmission levels within the study area.
source: Hence the observed differences in molFOB are likely to accurately reflect the relative differences in individual exposure as well as in population transmission levels within the study area.
evidence: The manuscript provides an assessment of the validity of molFOB comparisons despite potential biases.

claim: The incidence of clinical P. vivax episodes in this cohort was 0.16 clinical episodes/year in the placebo arm.
source: The very low incidence of clinical P. vivax episodes in our cohort, at 0.16 clinical episodes/year (placebo arm [Robinson et al., 2015]), contrasts drastically with that of 2.46 P. vivax clinical episodes/year observed in an earlier observational cohort of younger children aged 1–4 years from the same area (Lin et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific incidence data with citation.

claim: An earlier observational cohort of younger children aged 1–4 years from the same area had 2.46 P. vivax clinical episodes/year.
source: The very low incidence of clinical P. vivax episodes in our cohort, at 0.16 clinical episodes/year (placebo arm [Robinson et al., 2015]), contrasts drastically with that of 2.46 P. vivax clinical episodes/year observed in an earlier observational cohort of younger children aged 1–4 years from the same area (Lin et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites specific incidence data from a previous study for comparison.

claim: The 3-fold difference in Pv-molFOB between the two cohorts is modest compared to the 15-fold difference in the incidence of clinical Pv episodes.
source: The 3-fold difference in Pv-molFOB between the two cohorts seems modest when compared to the 15-fold difference in the incidence of clinical Pv episodes (Koepfli et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript compares differences in molFOB and clinical incidence between cohorts with citation.

claim: The much lower incidence of P. vivax clinical illness in 5–10 years old children is more likely explained by an advanced state of immunity to P. vivax compared to younger children than the drop in P. vivax transmission.
source: This suggests that the much lower incidence of P. vivax clinical illness in 5–10 years old children of this study is more likely explained by an advanced state of immunity to P. vivax compared to the younger children of the earlier cohort than the drop in P. vivax transmission.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the differences between cohorts.

claim: In a previous cohort study conducted in 2004 in 5–14 year old children in an area from PNG with substantially higher transmission levels, the risk of moderate- to high-density P. falciparum infections decreased significantly with age.
source: In a previous cohort study conducted in 2004 in 5–14 year old children in an area from PNG with substantially higher transmission levels (mean incidence risk 5.0 versus 0.8 infections/year, Michon et al., 2007; Robinson et al., 2015), the risk of moderate- to high-density P. falciparum infections decreased significantly with age (Michon et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study showing age-related patterns in a higher transmission setting.

claim: At heterogeneous transmission, changes of parasite prevalence and clinical episode incidence with age are less pronounced compared to settings with homogeneous transmission.
source: Mathematical modeling suggests that at heterogeneous transmission, changes of parasite prevalence and clinical episode incidence with age are less pronounced compared to settings with homogeneous transmission (Ross and Smith, 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites a modeling study describing effects of transmission heterogeneity on age patterns.

claim: In settings of decreasing and heterogeneous transmission, age alone may not be a suitable marker of immunity to P. falciparum.
source: In settings of decreasing and heterogeneous transmission, age alone may therefore not be a suitable marker of immunity to P. falciparum.
evidence: The manuscript provides an inference based on the observed patterns and cited literature.

claim: Combining age and molFOB to estimate cumulative life-time exposure may provide a more accurate surrogate measure of the extent of acquired clinical immunity.
source: Instead, combining age and molFOB to estimate cumulative life-time exposure may provide a more accurate surrogate measure of the extent of acquired clinical immunity.
evidence: The manuscript proposes an approach for better estimating immunity in heterogeneous transmission settings.

claim: Clinical P. falciparum incidence in cohort studies in children younger than 4 years from Maprik district had dropped from 2.56 clinical episodes/year before to 0.67 clinical episodes/year immediately after the free LLIN distribution campaign.
source: This delay in immune acquisition is however more than compensated by the overall much lower incidence of clinical malaria clinical episodes: in cohort studies in children younger than 4 years from Maprik district, clinical P. falciparum incidence had dropped from 2.56 clinical episodes/year before (observational cohort, [Lin et al., 2010; Mueller et al., 2012]) to 0.67 clinical episodes/year immediately after the free LLIN distribution campaign (placebo arm, [Betuela et al., 2012]).
evidence: The manuscript cites specific incidence data from studies before and after LLIN distribution.

claim: P. vivax and P. falciparum infections in this study were concentrated in the same children and villages.
source: P. vivax and P. falciparum infections in our study were concentrated in the same children and villages (Figure 3), likely due to overlapping focal transmission for P. falciparum and P. vivax and thus potentially high co-infection rates in mosquitoes.
evidence: The manuscript describes spatial patterns with reference to Figure 3 and provides an interpretation.

claim: The concentration of P. vivax and P. falciparum infections in the same children and villages is likely due to overlapping focal transmission and potentially high co-infection rates in mosquitoes.
source: P. vivax and P. falciparum infections in our study were concentrated in the same children and villages (Figure 3), likely due to overlapping focal transmission for P. falciparum and P. vivax and thus potentially high co-infection rates in mosquitoes.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the observed spatial patterns.

claim: An earlier cohort in younger PNG children found a decreased risk of P. falciparum clinical episodes after PQ radical cure.
source: Contrary to an earlier cohort in younger PNG children that found a decreased risk of P. falciparum clinical episodes after PQ radical cure (Betuela et al., 2012), we found indications for an increased risk of P. falciparum illness after clearance of P. vivax hypnozoites using PQ.
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study with contrasting findings.

claim: In individuals with substantial clinical immunity against P. vivax, a concurrent P. vivax infection may provide protection against P. falciparum clinical episodes by limiting P. falciparum densities.
source: Our data suggests that in individuals with substantial clinical immunity against P. vivax, a concurrent P. vivax infection may provide protection against P. falciparum clinical episodes by limiting P. falciparum densities (Table 6, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the observed associations with reference to tables.

claim: The comparable patterns of new mosquito-derived P. falciparum and P. vivax infections indicate that sustained use of LLINs results in a comparable reduction in transmission of both species.
source: The comparable patterns of new mosquito-derived P. falciparum and P. vivax infections indicate that sustained use of LLINs does result in a comparable reduction in transmission of both species.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the observed patterns in relation to LLIN use.

claim: The higher incidence and prevalence of P. vivax infections observed is directly linked to its ability to cause relapsing infections.
source: The higher incidence and prevalence of P. vivax infections observed in our data is thus directly linked to its ability to cause relapsing infections, highlighting the crucial role of hypnozoites for P. vivax epidemiology and the need to effectively intervene against these hidden stages.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation linking observed patterns to P. vivax biology.

claim: Hypnozoites play a crucial role for P. vivax epidemiology.
source: The higher incidence and prevalence of P. vivax infections observed in our data is thus directly linked to its ability to cause relapsing infections, highlighting the crucial role of hypnozoites for P. vivax epidemiology and the need to effectively intervene against these hidden stages.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation emphasizing the importance of hypnozoites.

claim: Discounting relapses, children acquired equal numbers of new P. falciparum and P. vivax blood-stage infections per year.
source: Discounting relapses, children acquired equal numbers of new P. falciparum (Pf) and Pv blood-stage infections/year (Pf-molFOB = 0–18, Pv-molFOB = 0–23) resulting in comparable spatial and temporal patterns in incidence and prevalence of infections.
evidence: The abstract summarizes key findings about equal acquisition of new infections when relapses are excluded.

claim: Including relapses, Pv-molFOB increased >3 fold relative to PQ-treated children.
source: Including relapses, Pv-molFOB increased >3 fold (relative to PQ-treated children) showing greater heterogeneity at individual (Pv-molFOB = 0–36) and village levels.
evidence: The abstract summarizes key findings about the impact of relapses on Pv-molFOB.

claim: Pf- and Pv-molFOB were strongly associated with clinical episode risk.
source: Pf- and Pv-molFOB were strongly associated with clinical episode risk.
evidence: The abstract summarizes key findings about the association between molFOB and clinical risk.

claim: Yearly Pf clinical incidence rate (IR = 0.28) was higher than for Pv (IR = 0.12) despite lower Pf-molFOB.
source: Yearly Pf clinical incidence rate (IR = 0.28) was higher than for Pv (IR = 0.12) despite lower Pf-molFOB.
evidence: The abstract summarizes key findings comparing clinical incidence rates between species.

claim: The relationships between molFOB, clinical incidence and parasite prevalence reveal a comparable decline in Pf and Pv transmission that is normally hidden by the high burden of Pv relapses.
source: These relationships between molFOB, clinical incidence and parasite prevalence reveal a comparable decline in Pf and Pv transmission that is normally hidden by the high burden of Pv relapses.
evidence: The abstract summarizes the main conclusion about comparable transmission decline.
